author: Annalisa Pardo
title: Las Cruces police officers detail juvenile crime issues to lawmakers - NewsBreak
text:
By Annalisa Pardo ,
29 minutes ago
LAS CRUCES, N.M. (KRQE) – Shocking and disturbing images showing just how violent some youth offenders are in New Mexico and how they mock the juvenile justice system. On Tuesday, the Las Cruces Police Department shared its findings with lawmakers and made its plea for changes to fix the problems during the next legislative session.
Story continues below
Photo after photo, headline after headline, LCPD Sergeant Mark Renteria and Officer Benjamin Berling shared with lawmakers the kind of crime and rhetoric they’re seeing from juvenile offenders who they said glorify gang lifestyle. “This is an issue where kids are killing each other, killing themselves, and killing innocent bystanders, and it’s happening repeatedly,” they said. They used images and jail call recordings to get their point across and shared how kids mock the system.
One text read, “lol bro, you get eight years at the most for murder here in New Mexico.”
On an audio recording, one juvenile said, “I’m just on 24-7 house arrest. I do whatever.”
LCPD said there is an issue with competency evaluations in the state system. They said many of the juveniles are deemed incompetent on the state level and released, but will be found competent and prosecuted on the federal level. “This is that revolving door. A child is arrested, charged, and then they’re released with no consequences, no treatment, no alternative. Released as if nothing happened to reoffend. And often that re-offense is an escalation in behavior. It gets worse,” the officers said.
LCPD is asking for a number of changes to help address violent youth crime, including updates to competency in the children’s code. They would like to address the difference in competency evaluations on the state and federal levels and give treatment options or alternatives to children found incompetent.
They’re also asking for more penalties for selling a gun without a background check. They also brought up more investment in juvenile probation officers so they could more easily issue arrest warrants if a juvenile violates their probation.
